```text
domain:
    # Matrix dimensions from PolyBench (M rows, N columns)
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index of A, B_in, B_out
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index of B_in, B_out
    k: dim in [0, M)          # reduction index over rows of A / B_in

data:
    # A is an M x M lower-triangular matrix with ones on the diagonal.
    # We store A in *column-major* layout so that accesses of the form A[k, i]
    # (k varying, i fixed) are unit-stride in memory, which matches the math
    # in the kernel and improves cache/TLB behavior and SIMD efficiency.
    A[row, col]: in DATA_TYPE = (row, col) -> col * M + row
        # col-major: element A[row, col] is at offset col*M + row

    # B_in is the original right-hand side matrix, M x N, in row-major layout.
    # Each row B_in[row, *] is contiguous in memory, so iterating over j
    # (columns) for fixed row is unit-stride.
    B_in[row, col]: in DATA_TYPE = (row, col) -> row * N + col

    # B_out is the output matrix, also M x N, in row-major layout.
    B_out[row, col]: out DATA_TYPE = (row, col) -> row * N + col

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters (compile-time constants
    # or runtime-tuned values chosen to match the target cache hierarchy
    # and SIMD width).
    TI: int > 0   # tile size for i (rows of A/B)    – e.g., 32 or 64
    TJ: int > 0   # tile size for j (columns of B)   – e.g., 64 or 128
    TK: int > 0   # tile size for k (reduction dim)  – e.g., 32 or 64
    VEC_J: int > 0  # SIMD width (in elements) along j – e.g., 8 or 16
    UK: int > 0     # unroll factor for innermost k loop – e.g., 4 or 8

computation:
    # Triangular matrix-matrix multiply:
    #
    #   B_out = alpha * A^T * B_in
    #
    # with A lower-triangular and diag(A) = 1.  From the original in-place
    # PolyBench kernel
    #   for i in [0, M):
    #     for j in [0, N):
    #       for k in [i+1, M):
    #         B[i][j] += A[k][i] * B[k][j];
    #       B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j];
    #
    # we can express the closed-form result as:
    #
    #   B_out[i, j] = alpha * (
    #       B_in[i, j] +
    #       sum_{k = i+1 .. M-1} A[k, i] * B_in[k, j]
    #   )
    #
    # There are no cross-row dependencies: all reads of B_in[k, j] use the
    # original B_in, so (i, j) iterations are fully independent and can be
    # freely reordered or parallelized.
    for i, j:
        B_out[i, j] = alpha * (
            B_in[i, j] +
            sum(k in [i + 1, M), A[k, i] * B_in[k, j])
        )

optimization:
    # ------------------------------
    # 1. Cache-aware blocking (tiling)
    # ------------------------------
    # Tile the (i, j) iteration space so that a block of rows of B_out and
    # the corresponding rows/columns of A and B_in fit into cache.
    #
    # I, J are tile indices; i, j become intra-tile coordinates.
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # Tile the reduction dimension k as well so that each (i-tile, k-tile)
    # of A and B_in fits in cache while we accumulate into a tile of B_out.
    # K is the tile index for k; k is the intra-tile index.
    block(k, K, TK)

    # ------------------------------
    # 2. Loop ordering / interchange
    # ------------------------------
    # Make tile loops outermost: iterate over tiles of rows (I) and columns (J),
    # then over tiles of the reduction dimension (K). This clusters work on
    # spatially close regions of A, B_in, and B_out.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # Inside each (I, J, K) tile, favor the order:
    #   i  (rows within tile)
    #   k  (reduction within tile)
    #   j  (columns within tile, unit-stride)
    #
    # Starting from the naive inner order (i, j, k), interchange the j and k
    # loops so that j becomes the innermost loop. This ensures that accesses
    # to B_in[k, j] and B_out[i, j] are along contiguous memory.
    interchange(k, j)

    # ------------------------------
    # 3. Parallelism
    # ------------------------------
    # Each (I, J) tile of rows and columns for B_out is independent, since
    # B_out[i, j] depends only on A and B_in. We can safely parallelize over
    # tiles of i (and optionally j) to exploit multiple cores.
    parallelize(I)

    # On systems with many cores, optional 2D tiling parallelization can be
    # enabled for better load balancing:
    parallelize(J)

    # ------------------------------
    # 4. SIMD vectorization
    # ------------------------------
    # Vectorize across j, the unit-stride (row-major) dimension of B_in/B_out.
    # This turns the inner loop over columns into SIMD operations that operate
    # on VEC_J elements per instruction.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # ------------------------------
    # 5. ILP in the reduction
    # ------------------------------
    # Unroll the innermost k loop to increase instruction-level parallelism
    # and better hide latency of dependent floating-point operations.
    unroll(k, UK)

    # ------------------------------
    # 6. Exploit triangular structure of A
    # ------------------------------
    # The reduction domain already starts at k = i+1, so we never touch the
    # structural zeros A[k, i] for k <= i (i.e., above the diagonal in A).
    # No additional work is needed beyond honoring the k in [i+1, M) bound;
    # this reduces the asymptotic work by about half vs. a full GEMM.
```

```text
domain:
    # M, N are problem sizes from PolyBench (M rows, N columns).
    i: dim in [0, M)      # row index (for A and B)
    j: dim in [0, N)      # column index (for B)
    k: dim in [0, M)      # reduction index over rows of A / B

data:
    # A is an M×M unit-lower-triangular matrix:
    #   A[i, j] = 0          for j > i
    #   A[i, i] = 1
    #   A[i, j] arbitrary    for j < i
    #
    # We conceptually store A row-major, but the optimization section
    # can change this layout if desired.
    A[i, j]: in num_t = (i, j) -> i * M + j   # row-major, lower-triangular with ones on diagonal

    # B_in is the original input matrix B (M×N) as read by the kernel.
    # We represent it as a separate logical array to make it explicit
    # that each output element depends only on the original B, which
    # enables full parallelism across (i, j). In an implementation,
    # B_in and B can alias safely if the schedule preserves that
    # snapshot semantics (as the Halide code does by using a separate
    # ImageParam and output Buffer).
    B_in[i, j]: in num_t  = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # row-major

    # B is the output matrix (same logical layout as B_in):
    #   B := alpha * (A^T * B_in), specialized to the PolyBench TRMM
    #   variant implemented here:
    #
    #   For each i, j:
    #     B[i, j] = alpha * ( B_in[i, j] +
    #                         sum_{k = i+1..M-1} A[k, i] * B_in[k, j] )
    #
    B[i, j]: out num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j     # row-major

parameters:
    alpha: num_t

computation:
    # Closed-form version of the original C kernel:
    #
    #   for (i = 0; i < M; i++)
    #     for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
    #       for (k = i+1; k < M; k++)
    #         B[i][j] += A[k][i] * B[k][j];
    #       B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j];
    #     }
    #
    # Because B[k][j] is always read from rows k > i that have not yet
    # been updated in that C loop nest, each final B[i, j] depends only
    # on the original B values, so we can express it in one expression
    # using B_in and compute all (i, j) in parallel.

    B_compute:
        for i, j:
            B[i, j] =
                alpha *
                ( B_in[i, j] +
                  sum(k in [i + 1, M),
                      A[k, i] * B_in[k, j]) )

dependencies:
    # Each B(i, j) depends only on A(:, i) and B_in(:, j) and is
    # independent of any other B(i', j'). This justifies aggressive
    # parallelization over i and j once B_in is treated as read-only.
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
        B_compute(i, j)  # no inter-(i, j) dependency; all outputs can be computed concurrently

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Promote the BLAS-3 style update order for better reuse.
    #
    # The naive interpretation of the formula would loop as:
    #   for i:
    #     for j:
    #       for k in [i+1..M):
    #         ...
    #
    # This yields poor cache usage for B_in[k, j] and A[k, i] (both have
    # large strides in k). We instead use a standard TRMM order inside
    # each (i-block), which iterates k outside j so that each row
    # B_in[k, *] is streamed contiguously:
    #
    #   for i:
    #     for j:                # initialize accumulators from B_in
    #       acc[i, j] = B_in[i, j]
    #     for k in [i+1..M):    # walk down column i of A
    #       a_ki = A[k, i]
    #       for j:              # contiguous row of B_in[k, *]
    #         acc[i, j] += a_ki * B_in[k, j]
    #     for j:
    #       B[i, j] = alpha * acc[i, j]
    #
    # This loop order is mathematically equivalent because the
    # multiplication-addition over (k, j) is associative and commutative
    # in (k, j), and it preserves the dependence on the original B_in.
    #
    # We express this using loop interchange within the reduction:
    interchange(j, k)
    # meaning: for each (i), iterate k outside and j inside when
    # evaluating the sum over A[k, i] * B_in[k, j].

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Cache-blocking (tiling) for all three dimensions.
    #
    # Introduce tunable tile sizes TI, TJ, TK chosen for the target
    # cache sizes (e.g., TI ≈ 32–64, TJ ≈ 64–256, TK ≈ 32–128).
    # This makes the kernel operate on submatrices that fit in the
    # higher-level caches, increasing reuse of A and B_in:
    #
    #   for I in tiles of i with size TI:
    #     for K in tiles of k with size TK:
    #       for J in tiles of j with size TJ:
    #         compute contributions from this (I, K, J) block to B.
    #
    block(i, I, TI)    # i = I * TI + i_local,    0 <= i_local < TI
    block(j, J, TJ)    # j = J * TJ + j_local,    0 <= j_local < TJ
    block(k, K, TK)    # k = K * TK + k_local,    0 <= k_local < TK

    # Hoist the tile loops to the outermost level so that we iterate in
    # the natural order: tiles of i, then tiles of k (panel along the
    # A column), then tiles of j (panel of B columns).
    hoist(I)
    hoist(K)
    hoist(J)

    # Within each (I, K, J) tile, the effective loop structure is:
    #   for i_local in [0, TI):
    #     for j_local in [0, TJ):
    #       acc = B_in[i, j]
    #     for k_local in [0, TK) with i < k:
    #       a_ki = A[k, i]
    #       for j_local in [0, TJ):
    #         acc[i_local, j_local] += a_ki * B_in[k, j]
    #     for j_local:
    #       B[i, j] = alpha * acc[i_local, j_local]

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Exploit multi-core parallelism.
    #
    # Because B(i, j) depends only on A and B_in and not on other
    # outputs, different (I, J) tiles can be computed independently.
    # Parallelize outer tiles; default is to use at least as many
    # threads as physical cores (here, up to 32) but not exceeding the
    # number of tiles:
    parallelize(I)     # distribute i-tiles across cores
    parallelize(J)     # additionally distribute j-tiles if M is small and N is large

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. SIMD vectorization along the contiguous B dimension.
    #
    # B_in and B are stored row-major, so j is the unit-stride
    # dimension. Vectorizing over j gives efficient SIMD loads/stores:
    #
    #   - For float:  V ≈ 8 or 16 (AVX2 / AVX-512)
    #   - For double: V ≈ 4 or 8
    #
    # We apply vectorization inside the innermost loops over j_local:
    vectorize(j, V)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Unroll short inner k loops for ILP within tiles.
    #
    # Inside each (I, K, J) tile, k_local ranges over TK. Choosing TK
    # to be a small multiple of the unroll factor allows the compiler
    # to schedule several independent FMA chains in parallel:
    #
    #   - Uk is small (e.g., 2–4) to avoid code-size explosion.
    #
    unroll(k, Uk)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Optional data-layout refinement (cache-friendly A and B_in).
    #
    # For even better memory behavior on some architectures, we can
    # change the physical layouts without altering the mathematical
    # meaning:
    #
    #   - Store A in column-major to make A[k, i] contiguous in k:
    #       A[i, j]: in num_t = (i, j) -> j * M + i
    #     This aligns accesses A[k, i] within a column i into sequential
    #     loads as k varies inside tiles.
    #
    #   - Optionally store B_in transposed (N×M) in column-major form so
    #     that B_in[k, j] is also contiguous in k when k is the inner
    #     loop in some microkernel variants:
    #       Bt[j, i]: in num_t = (j, i) -> j * M + i
    #       with B_in[k, j] = Bt[j, k]
    #
    # These layout changes are orthogonal to the algorithm above and
    # can be toggled depending on the target; they do not affect
    # correctness and keep extra storage under control because only one
    # extra transposed view is needed if chosen.
```

domain:
    # M: number of rows of A and B
    # N: number of columns of B
    i: dim in [0, M)        # row index in A and B
    j: dim in [0, N)        # column index in B
    k: dim in [0, M)        # reduction index over rows of A / B

data:
    # A is an M×M unit-lower-triangular matrix, stored row-major.
    #   A[row=i, col=k] is at offset i * M + k.
    # Initialization guarantees:
    #   - For all i, k: if k > i  then A[i, k] == 0        (above diagonal)
    #   - For all i:        A[i, i] == 1                   (unit diagonal)
    A[i, k]: in num_t = (i, k) -> i * M + k

    # B_in is the original M×N right-hand-side matrix, stored row-major.
    #   B_in[row=i, col=j] is at offset i * N + j.
    B_in[i, j]: in num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # B_out is the updated M×N result matrix, same layout as B_in.
    B_out[i, j]: out num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

parameters:
    alpha: num_t

computation:
    # Semantics: TRMM kernel
    #
    # Original C kernel (using 0-based indices, A is unit-lower-triangular):
    #
    #   for i in 0..M-1:
    #     for j in 0..N-1:
    #       for k in i+1..M-1:
    #         B[i][j] += A[k][i] * B[k][j];
    #       B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j];
    #
    # Careful dependence analysis + the invariants on A show that this is
    # equivalent to the following closed form that reads only the *original*
    # B (here called B_in) and writes a separate B_out:
    #
    #   B_out[i,j] = alpha * ( B_in[i,j] +
    #                          sum_{k=i+1..M-1} A[k,i] * B_in[k,j] )
    #
    # Because A is unit-lower-triangular:
    #   - A[k,i] == 0 for k < i (above the diagonal)
    #   - A[i,i] == 1
    #
    # we can also view this as a column-times-row product:
    #
    #   B_out[i,j] = alpha * sum_{k=0..M-1} A[k,i] * B_in[k,j]
    #
    # (since terms with k<i are multiplied by zero, and the term with k=i
    #  contributes A[i,i]*B_in[i,j] = 1 * B_in[i,j]).
    #
    # Here we keep the triangular domain explicit to mirror the original C:
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
        B_out[i, j] =
            alpha * (
                B_in[i, j] +
                sum(k in [i + 1, M),
                    A[k, i] * B_in[k, j]
                )
            )

dependencies:
    # Each (i,j) of B_out depends only on:
    #   - B_in[i,j] (the diagonal contribution),
    #   - A[k,i] and B_in[k,j] for k > i (strictly lower part of A).
    # Different (i,j) pairs are independent, so the update of B_out is
    # embarrassingly parallel over (i,j).
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
        B_in[i, j] -> B_out[i, j]
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N), k in [i + 1, M):
        A[k, i]   -> B_out[i, j]
        B_in[k, j] -> B_out[i, j]

optimization:
    # Overall aims:
    #   - Treat TRMM as a triangular variant of GEMM.
    #   - Improve cache locality via blocking (tiling) in i, j, and k.
    #   - Exploit parallelism across (i,j) tiles.
    #   - Vectorize along j (contiguous dimension in row-major B).
    #   - Keep the k-reduction register-resident and minimize memory traffic.
    #   - Respect the triangular structure of A (skip k ≤ i cheaply).
    #
    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters (chosen for a modern
    # 32-core x64 CPU; can be auto-tuned per machine):
    TI = 64    # tile size in i (rows of B, columns of A)
    TJ = 128   # tile size in j (columns of B)
    TK = 64    # tile size in k (reduction over rows of A / B)
    VJ = 8     # vector width in j (e.g., 8 floats or 4 doubles)

    # 1. Block (tile) the iteration space in i, j, and k for cache locality.
    #
    #    I, J, K are outer tile indices; i, j, k become inner indices within tiles.
    block(i, I, TI)      # i -> (I, i) with inner extent TI
    block(j, J, TJ)      # j -> (J, j) with inner extent TJ
    block(k, K, TK)      # k -> (K, k) with inner extent TK

    # 2. Hoist the tile loops to form a coarse-grain traversal.
    #
    #    After hoisting, the outer structure is:
    #      for I:
    #        for J:
    #          for K:
    #             for i in tile(I):
    #               for j in tile(J):
    #                 local reduction over k in tile(K), k > i
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # 3. Choose an inner loop order favorable for row-major B.
    #
    #    Inside each (I,J,K) tile, we want j innermost so that:
    #      - B_in[* , j] and B_out[* , j] are accessed with stride 1 in j,
    #      - k is the reduction dimension just inside (i,j).
    #
    #    Concretely, within a tile we want:
    #      for i in tile(I):
    #        for j in tile(J):   # innermost, contiguous
    #          accumulate over k in tile(K)
    interchange(i, j)    # make j the innermost non-reduction loop

    # 4. Vectorize across j (contiguous memory dimension in B_in/B_out).
    #
    #    This maps the innermost j-loop to SIMD instructions:
    #      - B_in[k, j..j+VJ-1] and B_out[i, j..j+VJ-1] become vector loads/stores.
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    # 5. Parallelize across (I,J) tiles.
    #
    #    Each (I,J) tile updates a disjoint submatrix B_out[i,j], so tiles can
    #    run in parallel with no write conflicts. We parallelize I first (rows),
    #    then J if additional parallelism is needed (e.g., large N).
    parallelize(I)
    parallelize(J)

    # 6. Reduce loop overhead in the k-reduction by unrolling within tiles.
    #
    #    The reduction over k is associative, so unrolling is valid.
    #    TK is large enough that unrolling by a small factor improves ILP
    #    without exploding code size.
    unroll(k, 4)

    # 7. Exploit the triangular structure of A inside tiles.
    #
    #    Within each (I, i) tile, valid k values satisfy k > i.
    #    Our TK-blocking may include some k ≤ i; we avoid wasted multiplies by
    #    guarding the inner update:
    #
    #      if k > i:
    #          accumulate A[k,i] * B_in[k,j]
    #
    #    #guard_k_triangle is a pseudo-optimization directive that inserts
    #    # this predicate in the innermost k-loop and allows the compiler
    #    # to eliminate fully-empty tiles when possible.
    #guard_k_triangle(i, k)  # only compute contribution when k > i

    # 8. Hoist invariants into registers to minimize memory traffic.
    #
    #    - alpha is invariant across all loops.
    #    - For fixed (K, k, J, j), B_in[k,j] is invariant across i; we can
    #      load it once per (k,j) and reuse it for all i in the current tile.
    #
    #    #hoist_invariant is a pseudo-optimization that tells the compiler
    #    # to lift these expressions out of inner loops:
    #hoist_invariant(alpha)
    #hoist_invariant(B_in[k, j])

    # 9. Optional fine-grain register blocking on i.
    #
    #    To increase reuse of B_in[k,j] and A[k,i] in registers while keeping
    #    cache footprint small, we can introduce a small inner block ii of i:
    II = 8
    block(i, ii, II)     # i -> (i, ii) with small register tile size
    unroll(ii, II)       # fully unroll the tiny ii-loop

    # Notes on memory usage:
    #   - We do not introduce any full-size auxiliary matrices: A and B_in are
    #     read-only; B_out is the only full-size output.
    #   - Any additional storage (e.g., for small register tiles implied by
    #     unrolling) is at most O(TI * TJ) and reused across tiles, so total
    #     peak memory is within 50% of the original A (M×M) + B (M×N) footprint.
    #
    # This results in a blocked, parallel, SIMD-accelerated TRMM kernel whose
    # memory-access patterns for A, B_in, and B_out are all cache-friendly,
    # while preserving the exact semantics of the original PolyBench TRMM
    # implementation.

domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index of A and B; also row index of the output
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index of B and of the output
    k: dim in [0, M)          # reduction index over rows of A and B

data:
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i + j * M
        # A is MxM, conceptually A[row=i][col=j].
        # Layout is column-major: for fixed column j, A[0..M-1, j] is contiguous in memory.
        # This makes accesses of the form A[k, i] (fixed i, varying k) contiguous in k.

    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i + j * M
        # B is MxN, conceptually B[row=i][col=j].
        # Also stored column-major: for fixed column j, B[0..M-1, j] is contiguous in memory.
        # Reads B[i, j] and B[k, j] and writes B[i, j] all use this same layout.

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE

computation:
    # Closed-form version of the original in-place PolyBench TRMM kernel:
    #
    #   for i in [0, M)
    #     for j in [0, N):
    #       for k in [i+1, M):
    #         B[i][j] += A[k][i] * B[k][j];
    #       B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j];
    #
    # All reads of B[*,*] in the inner loop reference the original input B,
    # not values updated in other (i, j), so we can express the final value
    # as a pure function of the inputs:
    #
    #   B_out[i,j] = alpha * ( B_in[i,j]
    #                         + sum_{k = i+1..M-1} A[k,i] * B_in[k,j] )
    #
    # Using that closed form removes loop-carried dependencies and exposes
    # full parallelism across (i, j).

    for i, j:
        B[i, j] = alpha * (
            B[i, j] +
            sum(k in [i + 1, M), A[k, i] * B[k, j])
        )

dependencies:
    # Semantically, the right-hand side uses the original B (as if it were a
    # distinct B_in array). There are no data dependences between different
    # (i, j) points:
    #
    #   for all (i1, j1) != (i2, j2):  B(i1,j1) does not depend on B(i2,j2)
    #
    # Therefore:
    # - All (i, j) iterations are independent and can be freely reordered.
    # - There are no true dependences along i or j, only within the reduction in k.
    #
    # The triangular constraint is entirely captured by the k-interval
    # [i+1, M), so no additional ordering constraints are required.

optimization:
    # --- Memory-layout rationale ------------------------------------------------
    # A and B are both column-major (row index i contiguous). For fixed i and j:
    #   - The reduction term uses A[k, i] and B[k, j].
    #   - With the chosen layout, both A[*, i] and B[*, j] are contiguous in k.
    #   - The inner reduction over k is thus a dot product over two contiguous
    #     vectors, ideal for SIMD.

    # --- Blocking for cache locality -------------------------------------------
    # Introduce blocking (tiling) in i, j, and k to improve cache reuse.
    # TI, TJ, TK are tunable constants (e.g., TI ≈ 64, TJ ≈ 32, TK ≈ 64),
    # chosen so that A- and B-panels operated on at once fit into LLC.
    block(i, I, TI)      # I: outer tile index over rows of A/B
    block(j, J, TJ)      # J: outer tile index over columns of B
    block(k, K, TK)      # K: inner tile index over reduction dimension

    # Resulting conceptual loop structure:
    #   for I in [0, ceil(M/TI)):
    #     for J in [0, ceil(N/TJ)):
    #       for i in I-tile:
    #         for j in J-tile:
    #           acc = B[i, j]                     # read original B
    #           for K in [0, ceil(M/TK)):
    #             # restrict to the valid triangular region k > i
    #             for k in intersection(K-tile, [i+1, M)):
    #               acc += A[k, i] * B[k, j]
    #           B[i, j] = alpha * acc             # write result

    # Hoist the tile indices to the outermost possible level so that blocking
    # is actually reflected in the execution order (i.e., apply loop interchanges
    # to get I, J, then inner i, j, K, k).
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # --- Parallelism ------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelize over row tiles; each worker gets a disjoint band of rows I
    # (and all columns J inside it). This gives good balance and avoids
    # false sharing since tiles of B are disjoint in memory.
    parallelize(I)

    # Optionally, if nested parallelism is efficient on the target, J can also
    # be parallelized, but typically a single parallel dimension suffices:
    # parallelize(J)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling -------------------------------------------
    # Vectorize the k-reduction: accesses A[k, i] and B[k, j] are contiguous in k,
    # so the compiler can generate SIMD dot-product style code.
    # V is a tunable SIMD width (e.g., 8 or 16 elements, matching AVX2/AVX-512).
    vectorize(k, V)

    # Unroll the remaining scalar k-iterations inside each K-tile to reduce loop
    # overhead and increase instruction-level parallelism. KU is a small factor
    # (e.g. 4 or 8) chosen so that KU * V does not exceed the cache line width.
    unroll(k, KU)

    # Within each (I, J) tile, vectorize across the row index i where possible:
    # B[i, j] is contiguous in i, and each (i, j) update is independent.
    # VI should divide TI and be compatible with the hardware SIMD width.
    vectorize(i, VI)

    # --- Notes on the triangular domain ----------------------------------------
    # - The triangular condition (k > i) is expressed directly in the reduction
    #   domain: k in [i+1, M).
    # - After blocking k into K and k, each K-tile only processes the subset of
    #   its k-range that satisfies k > i; iterations with k <= i are skipped.
    #   This avoids the wasted work present in a naive full-range reduction with
    #   a conditional inside the inner loop.
    #
    # - Because we use the closed-form expression w.r.t. the original B, this
    #   schedule is numerically equivalent to the original sequential TRMM kernel
    #   but exposes:
    #     * parallelism across (i, j) via tiles I (and optionally J),
    #     * SIMD parallelism along k (and optionally i),
    #     * improved cache reuse via blocking along i, j, and k.

```text
# Triangular matrix-matrix multiply (left, unit-lower, transposed):
#   B_out = alpha * A^T * B_in
#
# Original mathematical semantics (from the C kernel):
#   for i in 0..M-1:
#     for j in 0..N-1:
#       for k in i+1..M-1:
#         B[i][j] += A[k][i] * B[k][j];   # A is unit-lower: A[i][i] = 1
#       B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j]
#
# Closed-form (no in-place dependency across rows):
#   B_out[i,j] = alpha * ( B_in[i,j] +
#                          sum_{k=i+1..M-1} A[k,i] * B_in[k,j] )

domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index of B and of one dimension of A
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index of B
    k: dim in [0, M)          # row index used in the reduction

data:
    # A is an MxM unit-lower-triangular matrix.
    # We lay it out *column-major* so that the access pattern A[k, i] for
    # fixed i and increasing k is unit-stride in memory.
    #
    #   Physical offset = k + i * M
    #
    # Elements with k < i are defined but never used (or are zero); the
    # diagonal is 1.0 by construction of init_array().
    A[k, i]: in DATA_TYPE = (k, i) -> k + i * M   # column-major, triangular semantics

    # B_in is the original MxN right-hand side matrix.
    # We keep it in standard row-major order so that B_in[k, j] for fixed k
    # and increasing j is unit-stride in memory (good for vectorization).
    #
    #   Physical offset = i * N + j
    B_in[i, j]:  in  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

    # B_out is the resulting MxN matrix after TRMM:
    #   B_out = alpha * A^T * B_in
    # It can alias B_in in an actual implementation only if the loop
    # schedule preserves the original “read-only B_in” behavior; in this
    # model we treat it as a distinct output for clarity and to make
    # parallelization explicit.
    B_out[i, j]: out DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE          # scalar multiplier
    # Tuning parameters for blocking and vectorization (chosen for a
    # modern x64 CPU; values can be autotuned per machine):
    TI: int                   # tile size along i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    TJ: int                   # tile size along j (e.g., 128)
    VJ: int                   # vector width along j (e.g., 8 or 16, matching SIMD width)

computation:
    # Optimized algorithmic structure (equivalent to the original math):
    #
    # For each row i:
    #   1. Initialize B_out[i, j] from B_in[i, j].
    #   2. For each k > i, accumulate A[k, i] * B_in[k, j] into that row.
    #   3. Scale the completed row by alpha.
    #
    # This form:
    #   - avoids any in-place use of B_out in other rows (B_in is read-only),
    #   - groups operations into axpy-like row updates, which are cache and
    #     SIMD friendly (unit-stride in j),
    #   - uses the triangular property of A to avoid work for k <= i.

    for i in [0, M):
        # 1) Row initialization: copy the i-th row of B_in into B_out.
        for j in [0, N):
            B_out[i, j] = B_in[i, j]

        # 2) Triangular update: accumulate contributions from rows k > i.
        for k in [i+1, M):
            # A[k, i] is a scalar reused across all j for this (i, k).
            # Access is unit-stride in memory because A is column-major.
            let a_ki = A[k, i]
            for j in [0, N):
                # Unit-stride access in B_in and B_out along j.
                B_out[i, j] = B_out[i, j] + a_ki * B_in[k, j]

        # 3) Scale the entire row by alpha.
        for j in [0, N):
            B_out[i, j] = alpha * B_out[i, j]

optimization:
    # High-level parallelism:
    # -----------------------
    # Each row i of B_out depends only on row i and rows k > i of B_in,
    # and never on other rows of B_out, since B_in is logically read-only.
    # Therefore rows are independent and can be distributed across cores.
    #
    # We first tile the i dimension and then parallelize at the tile level
    # to generate sufficiently coarse-grained tasks for a 32-core CPU.

    block(i, I, TI)           # i = I * TI + i_inner, tiles of TI rows
    parallelize(I)            # run row tiles in parallel across cores

    # Cache and SIMD-friendly layout along j:
    # ---------------------------------------
    # For each fixed (i, k), the inner loop over j operates on contiguous
    # elements of B_in[k, j] and B_out[i, j]. We exploit this by tiling
    # and vectorizing j.

    block(j, J, TJ)           # j = J * TJ + j_inner, tiles of TJ columns
    vectorize(j, VJ)          # SIMD over j_inner inside each tile

    # Triangular reduction structure:
    # -------------------------------
    # The inner reduction is already restricted to k in (i+1 .. M-1); this
    # avoids unnecessary multiplies by zeros implied by the lower-triangular
    # structure of A. No explicit blocking of k is required for correctness,
    # but for very large M, an implementation may also choose:
    #
    #   block(k, K, TK)        # optional: tile k to improve A/B_in reuse
    #
    # as long as the triangular bound k > i is preserved inside each tile.

    # Loop ordering:
    # --------------
    # Within each (I, i_inner) tile of rows:
    #   - For each row i, we prefer the order:
    #       for k in [i+1, M):    # outer within row
    #         for J: for j_inner: # inner, vectorized
    #     rather than j outer, k inner. This converts the computation for
    #     fixed (i, k) into a daxpy-style update of a full row, maximizing
    #     reuse of the scalar a_ki and producing long, contiguous vector
    #     operations over j.

    interchange(k, J)         # for each i, move k outside of J/j_inner loops

    # Scalar hoisting:
    # ----------------
    # Hoist the load of A[k, i] (a_ki) out of the inner j loop; it becomes
    # a scalar multiplied with a vector B_in[k, J:j_inner] each time.
    hoist(k)                  # hoist invariant scalar a_ki above inner j loop

    # Optional further tuning:
    # ------------------------
    # - TI, TJ, VJ should be chosen based on cache sizes and SIMD width.
    # - If B_out aliases B_in in a particular implementation, then
    #   parallelization over i must be disabled or restricted to preserve
    #   the original in-place C semantics; with separate B_in/B_out this
    #   is not an issue.
```
